records.citation: James W. St. G. Walker, "Allegories and Orientations in African-Canadian Historiography: The Spirit of Africville," Dalhousie Review 77, no. 2 (1997): 155–178.

verification.checked_against: DalSpace (Dalhousie) repository record and full-text PDF
verification.note: Full text read. Walker identifies five "orientations" (not schools) in African-Canadian historiography, distinguished by the role assigned to Black people: Black Clients (focus on white justice and philanthropy), Black Victims, Black Achievers, Black Community (which coincided with the social history movement) and, in the 1990s, Black Survivors. Africville serves as allegory for the African-Canadian experience. Note: the request cited this as CHR 1999; the checked record is Dalhousie Review 1997. Re-read 2026-10-12 for this draft: Clients (Landon, Riddell; Stouffer 1992), Victims (Silverman 1985; "American scholars pointed the finger at the racist reality lurking behind the North Star mythology"), Achievers, Community (Black Power, Black pride, social history; Winks said The Black Loyalists ended the "victims" school), Survivors (Brand 1991). About 80 articles, 50 books and 40 graduate theses in two decades; black women receiving increasing attention. The further-reading list was used to corroborate several records.

records.citation: Barry Cahill, "The Black Loyalist Myth in Atlantic Canada," Acadiensis 29, no. 1 (1999): 76–87.

verification.checked_against: Acadiensis PDF (journals.lib.unb.ca article 10801; Érudit id acad29_1for01); OpenAlex W1842039563
verification.note: Full text read. Cahill argues that fugitive slaves were "a subcategory of 'Blacks' not 'Loyalists'"; that the Black Loyalist myth is "an invention of academic scholars" attuned to "the ideology and psychology of the civil rights and human rights movements of the 1960s and 1970s"; and that its "hegemony" sidelines the history of the enslaved. Its origins he locates in Walker's interpretation.

records.supports: The revisionist critique of the Black Loyalist interpretation.

verification.note: Full text read. records.supports: Walker's reply to Cahill and his account of the Black Loyalists' origins in the civil-rights era.
